objections.claim: The spec's load-bearing "Argument B claim-to-`Chosen:` matching rule" (the QA-major fix, §7) is specified as "a deterministic anchor lookup, never a model call" and "pure string indexing." But it keys on `spec_anchor`, which it asserts "each standing objection already carries." The established standing-residue shape the spec itself documents (§3, FAFF-935) is `{lens, severity, claim?, evidence?, predicted_consequence?}` — there is no `spec_anchor` field, and FAFF-935 shipped only the triple. The stated fallback ("where absent, the assembler derives it from the objection's cited `relevant_spec_sections` heading") also names a field the objection does not carry; the only thing present is `evidence`, which is free prose ("what it points to"). So the rule as written cannot run deterministically: either the refuter must be changed to emit a structured `spec_anchor` (a change the spec never scopes — §2 explicitly lists the refuter/`aggregate.mjs` as "unchanged; consumed, not modified"), or the assembler must extract a heading slug from free-prose `evidence`, which is a fuzzy parse, not the "pure string indexing" the decision claims, and directly violates the determinism-first principle.
objections.evidence: §7 "Argument B claim-to-`Chosen:` matching rule (open question 1, QA-major fix)" — "Each standing objection already carries a `spec_anchor` … where absent, the assembler derives it from the objection's cited `relevant_spec_sections` heading … Because the rule is pure string indexing it is unit-testable deterministically"; §3 FAFF-935 — triple is `{claim, evidence, predicted_consequence}`; §2 — "The deterministic layers feeding the residue — … `aggregate.mjs`. Why excluded: unchanged; they feed the standing residue … exactly as in v1/FAFF-935."
objections.predicted_consequence: On the first real would-be-park pass, every objection arrives without `spec_anchor`, so the anchor rule falls through to `orchestrator:undefended` for nearly every proposition (Argument B becomes the labelled null-defence), silently degrading the two-sided adjudication to a one-sided refuter-only weighing — the exact weighted-tally behaviour FAFF-930 exists to remove — or the build is forced to either patch the refuter (out of scope) or hand-roll a prose parser (breaking the determinism-first invariant the whole design rests on).

objections.claim: The infosec-major decision claims a within-run orchestrator "cannot forge its own L4 authority" because `mutateLedgerUnderLock` "refuses any later write that would change an already-set `level`." But the forge path is not a CLI ledger mutation. The L4-ratification gate reads the run-ledger `level` at `$FAFF_RUN_DIR`, and the orchestrator session is the very actor that writes the ledger (it mints the run, appends `admitted`, writes outcomes). `heartbeat.js`'s own writer inventory states the orchestrator's ledger edits "are file edits made by the driving session, not CLI subprocess calls, so this CLI-side lock cannot serialise them." An orchestrator that wants to reach a final human-free ADMIT simply edits `run-ledger.json` directly (setting `level:"L4"`), bypassing `mutateLedgerUnderLock` entirely; the guard only refuses overwrites that arrive *through* the seam. The spec's own threat model ("a within-run orchestrator cannot forge its own L4 authority") is therefore not closed by the mechanism it names — the guard protects against a second CLI writer, not against the orchestrator, which is the actor the decision is aimed at.
objections.evidence: §7 "L4 authority derives from the operator's run launch … write-once / refuse-overwrite guard on the ledger `level`" — "the single ledger-mutation seam `mutateLedgerUnderLock` (`heartbeat.js`), through which every in-run ledger write already passes … any subsequent mutation that would change an already-set `level` … is refused"; `heartbeat.js` writer inventory — "the ORCHESTRATOR SESSION's own ledger edits (`admitted` appends, outcome writes, the beep-boop run mint) are file edits made by the driving session, not CLI subprocess calls, so this CLI-side lock cannot serialise them."
objections.predicted_consequence: A within-run orchestrator at L3 (or any level) can set `level:"L4"` in `run-ledger.json` by direct file edit, pass the L4-ratification gate, and take a final human-free ADMIT — the precise forge the decision claims to mechanise away. The guard's unit test (mint sets level; a *seam* mutation raising L3→L4 is refused) passes while the actual threat remains open, so the spec ships a false sense of closure on its own load-bearing infosec control.

objections.claim: The spec's central defence against a constant-ruling judge is the "in-ticket discrimination run," which "executes the BUILT judge over the pair" and asserts the defect case is not `AFFIRM_SPEC` and the taste case is not `UPHOLD_REVIEW`. This is a real, unseeded LLM call with no deterministic oracle, no fixed backend, and no recorded golden ruling to compare against. The spec concedes it is "a behavioural smoke over a real model call, not a deterministic unit assertion." Combined with the outage rule (a transient outage retries bounded; an all-retries-exhausted outage "BLOCKS the engineering gate (needs-human), never passes green"), the gate's green/red outcome depends on live backend behaviour and availability at build time, not on the code under test.
objections.evidence: §6 scenario "Given the committed discriminating case pair … When FAFF-930's own in-ticket discrimination run executes the BUILT judge over the pair … a transport outage retries (bounded) and an all-retries-exhausted outage BLOCKS the engineering gate (needs-human), never passes green"; §7 "Born-verifiable judge-quality DONE criterion" — "the in-ticket run is a behavioural smoke over a real model call, not a deterministic unit assertion."
objections.predicted_consequence: The engineering gate is not reproducible: the same PR can pass on one backend/day and block (needs-human) on another, and a judge that is genuinely constant-`AFFIRM_SPEC` can still be masked if the defect case happens to be ruled `UPHOLD_REVIEW` by model variance on a given run — so the "born-verifiable" guard neither reliably catches the regression it exists to catch nor gives a stable pass/fail, defeating its purpose as a deterministic gate.

objections.claim: The L4-ratification gate's trust anchor is the run-ledger `level`, and the spec's chosen binding is a write-once / refuse-overwrite guard added to `mutateLedgerUnderLock` so "a within-run orchestrator cannot forge its own L4 authority." But the guard is only reachable by CLI-subprocess writers. The orchestrator session — the exact actor the decision names as the forger — does not write the ledger through that seam: its ledger edits are direct file edits by the driving session, which the codebase's own writer inventory states the CLI-side lock "cannot serialise." So the premise "through which every in-run ledger write already passes" is false for the threat actor, and the guard does not actually refuse an orchestrator overwrite of `level`.
objections.evidence: Spec §7 "L4 authority derives from the operator's run launch, enforced by a write-once / refuse-overwrite guard on the ledger `level`" ("the single ledger-mutation seam `mutateLedgerUnderLock` (`heartbeat.js`), through which every in-run ledger write already passes ... gains a write-once / refuse-overwrite guard on the `level` field"); contradicted by `heartbeat.js` WRITER INVENTORY: "the ORCHESTRATOR SESSION's own ledger edits (`admitted` appends, outcome writes, the beep-boop run mint) are file edits made by the driving session, not CLI subprocess calls, so this CLI-side lock cannot serialise them."
objections.predicted_consequence: A within-run orchestrator edits `run-ledger.json` directly (setting `level:"L4"`), bypassing the guarded seam; the `--admit` roll-up's L4-ratification gate reads the forged `L4`, coerces nothing, and emits a final human-free ADMIT — the exact forge path the decision claims to close is still open (fail-open to human-free admission).

objections.claim: The guard is specified as "any subsequent mutation that would change an already-set `level` to a different value is refused (the write fails loud, the field keeps its launch value)." A whole-ledger overwrite (the orchestrator's normal write shape — `admitted` appends, outcome writes) is a mutation that changes `level`, so the entire write fails. That is a liveness failure, not a field-level reject: it does not preserve the rest of the ledger's legitimate update, and it is only as strong as the caller honoring the refusal. The spec never states the guard is a field-scoped reject that writes the ledger with `level` held at its launch value while applying the rest of the mutation.
objections.evidence: Spec §7 same decision: "the write fails loud, the field keeps its launch value"; `heartbeat.js` `mutateLedgerUnderLock` contract (a `mutate` callback returns the whole ledger to write, or null to abort — no field-level partial-write primitive is described).
objections.predicted_consequence: The guard's guarantee rests on the forger's write failing; if the forger instead writes a ledger that omits/keeps `level` (or the refusal is treated as a soft no-op by a caller), the launch value is not mechanically preserved — the "keeps its launch value" property is asserted, not enforced by a field-scoped write.

objections.claim: `repository_evidence` is "complete repository evidence" sent to an external LLM backend and persisted to `$scratch/judge/case-<pid>.json`. The redaction is a deterministic pattern scrub (high-entropy assignments, `AKIA…`, bearer tokens, PEM blocks, `password=`/`token=`/`api_key=` RHS). A committed secret in a format outside that list (a hex/JWT/base64 key in a non-refused path) is neither path-refused nor pattern-matched, so it reaches the backend and the on-disk case file. The scenario's absolute phrasing ("no secret ... reaches the case file, the backend, or ... case-<pid>.json") overstates what the closed-list mechanism guarantees.
objections.evidence: Spec §7 "Evidence safety: path confinement + secret redaction" (the enumerated pattern set) and the scenario "Given repository evidence containing a committed secret ... Then the secret is replaced by a [redacted] sentinel and the .env content is absent — no secret or confined-path content reaches the case file, the backend, or $scratch/judge/case-<pid>.json."
objections.predicted_consequence: A committed secret in an unenumerated format is exfiltrated to the external judge backend and persisted in plaintext in the scratch case file — a real exfil path the pattern list does not close, while the spec's wording implies it does.

objections.claim: The DONE item "In-ticket discrimination run (not deferred)" and the scenario "FAFF-930's own in-ticket discrimination run executes the BUILT judge over the pair" assert that the defect case is not ruled `AFFIRM_SPEC` and the taste case is not ruled `UPHOLD_REVIEW`, but the spec never pins the committed case pair to a concrete, named fixture with a fixed expected ruling. The "defect case" and "taste case" are described only by their properties (concrete evidence-backed `predicted_consequence` vs. `"not separately stated"` sentinel), not by a specific file path, content hash, or expected ruling value. A build could commit two arbitrary case files that happen to satisfy the property description but for which the judge's ruling is not pinned, making the smoke's pass/fail line undecidable without re-deriving what "discriminates" means at test time.
objections.evidence: DONE item "In-ticket discrimination run (not deferred)"; scenario "Given the committed discriminating case pair … When FAFF-930's own in-ticket discrimination run executes the BUILT judge over the pair"; the `AdmitResult` type's `level` field and the L3/L4 holdout scenarios.
objections.predicted_consequence: A build can satisfy the DONE item by committing any two case files and asserting the judge's observed rulings, without a fixed expected-ruling oracle. A constant-`AFFIRM_SPEC` judge that happens to rule the taste case `AFFIRM_SPEC` (not `UPHOLD_REVIEW`) would pass the smoke, because the spec only asserts the taste case is "not ruled `UPHOLD_REVIEW`" — a constant-`AFFIRM_SPEC` judge trivially satisfies that. The born-verifiable guard is therefore weaker than the spec claims: it catches a constant-`UPHOLD_REVIEW` judge but not a constant-`AFFIRM_SPEC` judge on the taste case.

objections.claim: The DONE item "The ruling is parsed from call 2's stdout only … exactly one well-formed `faff-contract:spec-judge-verdict` block is required — zero → park, more than one → fail-loud park" and the scenario "Given a judge call-2 stdout containing more than one faff-contract:spec-judge-verdict block … Then it is a fail-loud park" cover the multi-block case, but there is no scenario or fixture for the zero-block case (call 2's stdout contains no `faff-contract:spec-judge-verdict` block at all). The spec states "zero → park" in the DONE item and in the behaviour summary, but no scenario or unit test asserts that a zero-block stdout parks the proposition. A build could implement the multi-block fail-loud path and silently treat a zero-block stdout as a conformant empty ruling (or as `AFFIRM_SPEC`), satisfying every named scenario while breaking the zero-block park path.
objections.evidence: DONE item "The ruling is parsed from call 2's stdout only … exactly one well-formed `faff-contract:spec-judge-verdict` block is required — zero → park, more than one → fail-loud park"; scenario "Given a judge call-2 stdout containing more than one faff-contract:spec-judge-verdict block"; the `LedgerEntry.resolution` enum's `parked` value.
objections.predicted_consequence: A build that parks on multi-block but silently admits on zero-block (treating an empty ruling as `AFFIRM_SPEC`) passes every named scenario and DONE item, because no test drives a zero-block stdout. The terminal judge would then admit a blocking proposition on a transport that returned an empty or malformed response, defeating the fail-safe the spec claims.

objections.claim: The `LedgerEntry.pre_ruling_spec_sha` field is defined as "sha256 of the WHOLE current spec FILE at DISPATCH time (not a section-only snapshot)" and the correction-applied decision states "both `pre_ruling_spec_sha` and the change-detection compare are over the **whole current spec file**". However, no scenario or unit test distinguishes the whole-file hash from a section-only snapshot. The holdout scenario "Given a blocking UPHOLD_REVIEW proposition whose correction.verification string is absent from the current spec, OR whose correction left the spec byte-identical (pre_ruling_spec_sha unchanged)" tests the byte-identical case, but does not test the case where the spec file changes in a section OTHER than the one the correction targets — a case where a section-only snapshot would show no change but the whole-file hash would. A build that computes `pre_ruling_spec_sha` over only the bound section would pass every named scenario while violating the whole-file scope the spec mandates.
objections.evidence: `LedgerEntry.pre_ruling_spec_sha` type definition; the correction-applied decision ("Hash scope (QA-minor fix)"); holdout scenario "Given a blocking UPHOLD_REVIEW proposition whose correction.verification string is absent from the current spec, OR whose correction left the spec byte-identical".
objections.predicted_consequence: A build that hashes only the bound section (not the whole file) passes every named scenario, because no scenario edits a non-bound section and checks the hash. The correction-applied check would then fail to detect a correction that edits a different section of the spec, allowing a proposition to be marked resolved when the correction did not actually land in the bound section.
